rationale: B wins because it keeps four clean, pitchable lanes and makes the risk explicit instead of decorating the announcement. Its strongest line, "Mercury says it's profitable on 200,000 businesses. Consumer banking will test that claim," turns the missing economics into the story. A has good bones, but "When a business-only fintech decides it's ready to be a full-service bank" is the extra plate at the buffet: overclaimed, thinly pegged, and half-admitted as an n-of-1 trend.
gaps_in_A: "full-service bank" overstates the facts. Mercury is offering consumer checking and savings through partner banks, not becoming a chartered full-service bank.
"A profitable business bank is wading into the notoriously thin margins of consumer banking" imports industry context not supplied in the update and risks sounding smarter than the evidence.
"start narrow with businesses, expand into consumer once profitable" is framed as a possible playbook before the proof exists; A admits it needs another example, which means the angle is not ready.
"the bank Silicon Valley Bank's collapse built" is sharp, but imprecise: Mercury is not itself a bank charter, and the update says SVB made it well known, not built it from scratch.
gaps_in_B: "The launch is live today" is a little too definitive. The update says Mercury is launching at the current time, but does not explicitly say public/live today.
"Mercury wants to hold consumers' money without being a bank" is a useful pressure headline, but legally sloppy unless the copy immediately clarifies partner banks hold deposits.
"betting that name works on consumers" is a fair inference, not a stated fact; it needs an executive quote or distribution detail before becoming the pitch spine.

The counterposition angle asks for "what Mercury Personal does that existing consumer accounts don't," but the supplied facts contain no feature differentiation, so that angle can collapse into generic launch coverage fast.
